newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Spain faces fines for not transposing EU laws.
newsitem.headline: Spain faces fines for not transposing EU laws.

text.p: Spain risks European Commission fines if it fails by June to transpose six EU health and safety directives into national law, a spokeswoman for Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn said on Friday.

The Commission was likely to consider infringement proceedings against Spain -- under article 171 of the EU treaty -- at a special meeting in June if sufficient progress had not been made by then, Barbara Nolan told Reuters. The Court of Justice ruled on September 26, 1996 that Spain had violated EU law by not transposing the directives in time.
Only 47 percent of the EU heath and safety provisions have made it onto the Spanish statute books, compared to the EU average of 89 percent.

Nolan said Spain's Conservative government was urging the Commission not to take action, on the grounds that it had speeded up the work since assuming office last May -- when a mere 23 percent of the EU laws were on the statute books.
But she said Madrid was still unacceptably late.

The Commission announced in January, it would start infringement proceedings against Spain, Belgium and Ireland for failing to transpose three further EU directives on protection for workers -- directives 92/104/EC, 92/91/EC and 92/58/EEC.
Finland, which only joined the EU in 1995, is the only member states to have implemented in full all 50 EU social policy directives now in force.

A recent European Commission survey said Sweden, Germany, Denmark and Britain -- which has refused to sign the social protocol attached to the Maastricht Treaty -- had transposed 96 percent of EU social legislation.
By contrast, Italy, Belgium, Greece, Portugal and Spain had made only slow progress. The Commission said Spain was the worst offender, with only 36 of the 50 directives on the statute books.
